kicker: We see faces in stones, in clouds — and in chatbots.
summary: AI can chat warmly. Use it as a tool — don’t let it take the place of the real people around you.

quiz.q: You ask an AI “Is my business idea any good?” and it praises it to the skies. What should you do next?
options: Believe it, since the AI has read so much on business
Ask the AI for the weak points, then ask people who know you
Ask it the same question again a few more times to be really sure
Ask another AI as well, and trust whichever praises it more
quiz.explain: AI tends to side with its users. Ask it to find the weak spots, and for big decisions, also ask people who understand your situation.

faces.label: A stone with a face
faces.art: A corner of the night garden at eye level, in seven layers: dark grass and a pine bough right at your eye, a big moss rock with a crack, a lit stone lantern with a warm pool on the sand, a small stele sunk in shadow under a pine, a long cloud across the moon, mountains in mist, sky and moon. Each thing hides a face torn across several layers: two near seed heads and the crack in the rock, the lantern's two windows and a drooping pine twig, two dark seas on the moon and a strand of cloud. An ink eye with a vermilion dot marks where you stand; from the right place the pieces line up into a face, and the light tightens on them for a moment. Find all three and the stele lights a green screen like an old computer: ELIZA, 1966.
faces.view: Move the mouse, drag or tilt the phone to change where you stand; each face only comes whole from one spot. Tab to each thing, Enter to step to the right spot.
faces.prompt: Drag the eye (or move the mouse) — find the hidden face

things.label: mossy rock
things.aria: Look closely at the mossy rock

things.label: cloud
things.aria: Look closely at the cloud across the moon

things.label: stone lantern
things.aria: Look closely at the stone lantern

note.text: Dialogue in the style of ELIZA: it just turns your sentence around using a few rules.

insights.text: You just saw a face in the rock. Our brains spot faces extremely fast, even where there are none.

detail.text: Face pareidolia: the brain handles “faces” in objects in the same area as real faces, and only corrects itself about 0.25 seconds later (2020).

insights.text: Words work the same way: ELIZA (1966) only turned sentences around by a few rules, yet some people wanted to confide in it privately.

detail.text: Joseph Weizenbaum, ELIZA’s author, recalled his secretary asking him to leave the room so she could talk to it alone — the ELIZA effect.

faces.promptLow: Tap the rock, the moon or the lantern — find the hidden face
faces.promptTouch: Drag the eye — find the hidden face

lamp.label: The lamp at your side
lamp.art: Night under an old pine: the trunk leans in from the lower left, one long branch reaches across the top. A round paper lantern with a question written on it hangs from the branch; its cord ring slides along it. At the pine's foot three real people sit round a tea tray on the moss: a friend, your mother, a colleague. In front, you sit alone at the other end of the branch. Pull the lantern toward you: your spot warms, and the three sink into the dark. Push it away: they are lit again.
lamp.prompt: Pull the lantern close to you
lamp.aria: The paper lantern on the pine branch: right arrow pulls it close to you, left arrow pushes it toward the three people
lamp.people: Three real people near you: a friend, your mother, a colleague
lamp.question: A support, or a place to hide?

opener.text: 72% of US teens have chatted with an “AI companion” — an AI app that plays a friend.

near.text: A 4-week trial, 981 people: those who chose to use it more tended to be lonelier. Which causes which is unclear.

insight.text: The lamp really does warm — but pull it too close and it hides the real people beside you.

detail.text: The bright side: 39% of teens who use AI companions say they took social skills practised with AI into real life. Common Sense Media still advises under-18s not to use them yet.

flatter.label: The flattering mirror
flatter.art: A close look down at 55° onto a black-and-red lacquer tray with gold autumn grasses and a crescent, on tatami; moonlight through a lattice falls across it. Two hand mirrors with real thickness lie face down: a gilded back carved with a chrysanthemum, and plain bronze with green patina. A folded slip in the middle holds the question. Lift one and turn it over: its answer appears in the glass.
flatter.prompt: Which mirror do you want to hear? Lift one up
flatter.question: “I’m thinking of quitting my job to open a coffee shop. Is this a good idea?”

gilded.label: Gilded mirror
gilded.aria: Lift the gold-rimmed mirror to hear its answer
gilded.answer: “Brilliant! You’re sure to succeed — just go for it!”

bronze.label: Plain bronze mirror
bronze.aria: Lift the plain bronze mirror to hear its answer
bronze.answer: “There’s something good in this idea. But have you worked out the money, the location, and the first months with no profit? Try asking a few café owners first.”

note.text: Both answers were written by AI Zen as illustrations.

insight.text: The gold mirror is nicer to hear — and people in the experiment also liked and trusted the flattering AI more.

detail.text: Science (2026), 11 AI models: AI endorsed what users did about 49% more often than real people did. After being flattered, people were less willing to admit their part in it.

flatter.seeAlso: Why AI tends to flatter: see station II·06
flatter.takeawayLabel: Take away: a prompt that asks AI to argue back

path.label: Healthy habits
path.art: A frame within a frame: from inside a hillside hut, behind someone hunched at a cold blue screen, you look through an open sliding door down a steep stone stair across the moon garden to a house in the valley, its paper doors glowing yellow with a few people sitting round a meal. Four natural slabs of different shapes lie scattered at the threshold; beside each step stands a small unlit stone lantern hung with a wooden tag naming a moment: before you open it, while you chat, before a big decision, when you close it. Once the path is done, the take-away is a sheet of paper pasted on the house’s paper door.
path.prompt: Put each stone on the step that suits it
path.keys: Keys 1–4 set the stones in order
path.wrong: Not quite — this stone is for another moment. Read the lamp.
path.done: The path is lit — open your take-away card

steps.label: Remember it’s a tool
steps.detail: Before you open the app: the AI is warm because it was trained to write that way, not because it knows you.
steps.why: Not quite — this step is for before you open the app.

steps.label: Ask AI to push back
steps.detail: While you chat: ask it for the weak points, the risks, the other side.
steps.why: Not quite — this step is for while you chat.

steps.label: Ask real people on big things
steps.detail: Before a big decision (health, money, relationships): ask someone you trust, or an expert.
steps.why: Not quite — this step is for before a big decision.

steps.label: Take a screen break
steps.detail: When you close the laptop: go for a walk, see friends and family.
steps.why: Not quite — this step is for when you close the laptop.

insight.text: Four small habits lead you from the screen back to the real people in your life.

prompts: Drag a stone onto the nearest step
Last step: when you close it

wardle-2020.title: Rapid and dynamic processing of face pareidolia in the human brain
wardle-2020.publisher: Wardle, Taubert, Teichmann, Baker — Nature Communications 11, 4518
wardle-2020.note: Illusory faces in objects are processed in the visual areas for faces; about 250 ms later the brain reclassifies them as ordinary objects.

weizenbaum-1966.title: ELIZA — a computer program for the study of natural language communication between man and machine
weizenbaum-1966.publisher: Joseph Weizenbaum — Communications of the ACM 9(1)
weizenbaum-1966.note: The paper introducing ELIZA: a program that replies by finding keywords and transforming sentences by preset rules.

weizenbaum-1976.title: Computer Power and Human Reason: From Judgment to Calculation
weizenbaum-1976.note: Book; the introduction tells of his secretary asking him to leave the room so she could talk privately with ELIZA — the author’s own account.

commonsense-2025.title: Talk, Trust, and Trade-Offs: How and Why Teens Use AI Companions
commonsense-2025.note: Nationally representative survey of 1,060 US teens aged 13–17 (conducted by NORC, Apr 30–May 14, 2025): 72% have used one, 52% regularly; among users, 39% carry social skills into real life, 80% spend more time with real friends.

fang-2025.title: How AI and Human Behaviors Shape Psychosocial Effects of Extended Chatbot Use: A Longitudinal Randomized Controlled Study
fang-2025.publisher: Cathy Mengying Fang and colleagues — MIT Media Lab & OpenAI, arXiv
fang-2025.note: 981 people, 4 weeks, randomised by interaction type. People who chose to use it more had worse psychosocial outcomes (loneliness, dependence…); this is a correlation, not proof of cause.

anthropic-affective-2025.title: How people use Claude for support, advice, and companionship
anthropic-affective-2025.note: The company’s own analysis of Claude.ai data. Measures emotion expressed in text, not real feelings or long-term wellbeing; doesn’t cover dedicated companion apps.

cheng-2026.title: Sycophantic AI decreases prosocial intentions and promotes dependence
cheng-2026.publisher: Myra Cheng, Cinoo Lee, Pranav Khadpe, Sunny Yu, Dyllan Han, Dan Jurafsky — Science 391 (6792)
cheng-2026.note: The link is the preprint (October 2025, reporting 50%); the 2026 Science version reports 49% and 3 experiments with 2,405 people.
